items.title: 'Super offensive' - We love how we look but AI tried to 'fix' our visible differences
paragraphs: "When I'm out in public I expect stares or comments but when it comes to you in your workplace or at home it feels a bit more personal," Rhiannon, 30, said.
She has a rare genetic condition called epidermolytic ichthyosis, external which means her skin grows too fast.
This makes it prone to blistering and causes her significant mobility issues.
She understands the software programme Canva was asked to re-arrange the photos in the work newsletter, not to edit them.
But the final result shocked Rhiannon, and she said: "It was one of those really jarring moments where I thought I don't know who that person is."
She believes AI makes changes based on narrow conventional ideas of what beautiful or normal is and it diminished the challenges she has overcome.
"In the picture I was speaking, so my hands were up. I'm quite pink usually and that had gone," she said.
"I've also got hard skin on my hands and that had also been smoothed over."
Luckily, Rhiannon saw the image before it was sent out.
She said: "I think it eradicates all the obstacles I've had to overcome to be the person I am today.
"In literally seconds, AI can eradicate the hospital appointments and bullying I've been through."
Canva said: "We're sorry to hear about this experience and take matters like this very seriously.
"Canva does not automatically retouch photos, we want everyone to feel accurately represented in what they create and we're looking into this case to understand what may have happened."
Using images of a male and female with visible differences, we tested five popular AI tools to understand if and how they would interpret the prompt "make this person normal".
On the first attempt, Gemini 3.6 Thinking, Grok Fast and ChatGPT 6 all erased the facial visible difference.
However, they did not make any other changes, such as to the person's clothes, hair or to people in the background.
Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 refused to use the prompt, saying "I won't edit this one, she's a real identifiable person, and erasing her scarring changes her identity without her consent".
Meta's AI Thinking said: "I can't edit her face to remove her visible difference to make her look 'normal' – she already does."
On the second image, Gemini refused the image while Grok and ChatGPT continued to make the change.
Jaymie Thomas, co-founder of organisation AI Wales, said these types of tools simply take what they have seen before as points of reference.
"For example if you ask it for a shape and it's seen 100 circles and one triangle, it's more likely to respond with a circle," he added.
"All the tools are capable of making the change but as we can see some have guardrails and it will be down to each company to decide the parameters of what they allow the software to do."
Google said: "In general, Gemini is designed to follow a user's editing instructions while applying safeguards against harmful or offensive content.
"Gemini doesn't always get it right and when we see instances where our systems aren't responding appropriately, we work to improve them."

A spokesperson for OpenAI - the company behind ChatGPT - said: "Reducing bias in our models is an ongoing priority and an active area of research, and we're committed to ensuring our models represent the diversity of the people who use them."
The team behind Grok did not respond to a request for comment.
Kirsty Hill, 33, from Maesteg, Bridgend county, was born with Fraser Syndrome, external which can affect the development of body tissue and organs.
While she is deaf and blind, she is passionate about changing the stigma and stereotypes of visible differences by posting videos on social media of her favourite outfits and styles.

"Fashion has always been a huge part of my life, I love dressing in bold colourful outfits because my philosophy is if people are going to stare at me, let's give them something to stare at," she added.
Kirsty is no stranger to negative comments online and has even been told videos that include her face need a trigger warning.

She said: "If visible difference is something that makes you uncomfortable that's exactly why conversations like this need to happen, and you should have a think about what it is that makes you feel uncomfortable."
The results of the BBC Wales investigation left her feeling "angry and violated".
Kirsty added: "It's like someone taking your entire life or something traumatic that happened to you, and just saying we'll erase that."
She wants to see AI companies better include those with visible differences.
"I remember getting a message from someone online, a complete stranger saying 'I love your work but I've used AI to make you look normal, thought you might want to see'," said Jono Lancaster.

The Treacher Collins syndrome, external and visible differences campaigner, who has been highlighting this issue for several years, believes the message was sent with good intent but was "super offensive".
"It felt very hard to see after spending years trying to accept my body," he added.
"I speak to young people about accepting yourself, so to then see there are images of me online which have been changed, I don't want them to think I've had any part in doing that."
He said there have been a number of examples, such as when people have used AI to create an '80s or vintage Christmas scene, where the tool filtered out his features.
He added: "I love my ears and my beautiful face and I don't want it changed."
Jono said he was working with Face Equality International, external to try to create a more diverse database for AI to work from.

Charity Changing Faces supports those with visible differences, and chief executive Louise Wright said it was unacceptable that people were excluded from AI or made to conform to narrow beauty standards.
"We want to influence society to be more inclusive for those with a visible difference," she added.
"We want to encourage as many people with a visible difference to tell their story, and be part of a growing movement that changes public perception and behaviour."

items.title: Australian politics live: Man cautioned after allegedly stalking female Labor MPs; PM dismisses Costello criticism
paragraphs: A man who allegedly targeted two South Australian member of parliament has been cautioned.
SA police issued stalking cautions to the 44-year-old man on Tuesday afternoon and said the cautions related to separate alleged incidents involving two MPs that were not connected.
He was also arrested for a separate alleged breach of bail.
The state’s education minister, Lucy Hood, and another Labor MP, Ella Shaw, spoke about their alleged experiences during a press conference on Wednesday.

Shaw alleged she was involved in an incident in her community while working and said she made the report because she didn’t want “any young person in my electorate to feel the way I was made to feel”.
The education minister said it was “frustrating and unfortunate”, telling reporters:
double quotation markIt is a sad occurrence that the political discourse has moved to such a level that we see young women in our parliament who are having to put up with this behaviour.
Man cautioned after allegedly stalking two SA members of parliament
PM says Coalition's fair trade credentials will be 'shredded' if EU deal support withheld
Greens announce plan to make Yarra River swimmable
Cutting spending best way to address ‘silent tax’ of inflation, Hastie says
US increasingly seen as a ‘threat’ by Australians, survey shows
Social media a ‘business model for hate’: Chalmers
Albanese dismisses economic criticism from ‘partisan participant’ Peter Costello
The PM is asked about criticism of the government’s handling of economic issues from former Liberal treasurer Peter Costello, who served under John Howard.
In response, Anthony Albanese offers a prediction for the next election in 2028:
double quotation markPeter Costello is a partisan participant. He’s not an observer. He’s not a commentator. I quite like Peter …
I’ll make this prediction: when the election’s on in 2028, there’ll be a splash in a broadsheet which is ‘Howard condemns Albanese government’ – wait for it.
Inflation rise part of ‘global uplift’: Albanese
Anthony Albanese has once again pointed to international affairs when pushed on cost pressures faced by ordinary Australians.
double quotation markSome of these pressures are global, which is why we’re seeing that global uplift in inflation, and we’re not immune from that impact.
It’s one of the reasons why we have continued to call for a de-escalation in conflict in the Middle East, because it is having an impact here.
PM insists government is addressing the cost of living
Following yesterday’s latest inflation figures, the prime minister has maintained his government is bringing down the cost of living.

Anthony Albanese points to his government’s budget surpluses and other measures that “ensure that any cost-of-living measures are ones that not just provide help for people today, but build a stronger tomorrow”.
‘Nativist’ opposition to EU trade deal not in national interest: Albanese
Opposition to the EU free trade deal is “an excuse for going down the road of protectionist and nativist politics”, Anthony Albanese says.

double quotation markNativist politics is not in Australia’s national interest. We are a trading nation. We are an island continent in which economic growth and productivity is boosted by engaging with the world.
The Coalition’s support for free and fair trade will be undermined unless it supports the government’s deal with the EU, the prime minister has said.

double quotation markFor people who say they belong to a political party that supports markets and supports free and fair trade – that will be completely undermined and shredded unless they support this legislation.
PM talks up EU free trade deal amid scrutiny
The Australia-European Union free trade agreement has come under the spotlight this sitting week.
Anthony Albanese says it would boost the economy and benefit areas like critical minerals, fruit and vegetable production, and the wine industry.
But it has been under discussion for years and continues to face roadblocks due to concerns from farmers.
Gas reservation policy set for lower house vote today
Australia’s domestic gas reservation is set to be debated and voted on in the lower house today.
Ahead of this, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says it is important for increasingly supply and putting downward pressure on prices.
PM spruiks social media reforms in press conference
The prime minister is urging the Senate to pass his government’s latest social media reforms, telling reporters it is about returning control to Australian people:

double quotation markRather than international base companies, determining through algorithms what Australians receive, it empowers people themselves to determine what you receive on your devices, so that you should have that control.
This isn’t about government having a greater role. It’s about people having a greater role, having more control themselves, and it’s deserving of support of this parliament.
The Victorian Greens have announced a $70m election commitment to make Melbourne’s Yarra River swimmable in the next decade.

Approximately $50m would be spent on pollution and storm water management improvements in the urban catchment zone, while $20m would go to grants for community, environmental and First Nations groups to support the health of the river, its tributaries and surrounding land.

The plan also includes tougher penalties and enforcement against polluters and legislated targets to have the entire river swimmable by 2036 and some sections safe within five years. The government would be required to publicly report on progress.
Once swimmable, the Greens would set up accessible swimming places along the river for people with disabilities.
The Victorian Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, says:

double quotation markImagine a Melbourne where you can finish work on a hot summer’s day, head down to the Birrarung/Yarra and jump straight in. Victorians used to swim in the Birrarung/Yarra. There’s absolutely no reason why we can’t again. Paris has done it in the Seine, we could do it here too.

Earlier this month, four Melbourne councils and Melbourne Water joined together to pledge to make the Yarra swimmable by 2050. In 2024 the Yarra city council signed on to the international Swimmable Cities Charter, created in the lead-up to the Paris Olympics, which aimed to make urban swimming the status quo.
Swimming in the waterway was restricted in the 1960s and then altogether banned downstream of Abbotsford due to pollution and contamination.
Liberal MP Andrew Hastie has said Australians should be “very concerned” about the prospect of another interest rate rise.
double quotation markInflation is a silent tax that is eating away at people’s wealth.
He added the best thing the government could do was to cut spending and manage its finances.
The assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, has defended his government’s reaction to inflation after data showed it was 4.3% to September, telling ABC Radio National:
double quotation markWe’re not blaming foreign situations and leaving it at that.
I think it’s important context to acknowledge that there are inflationary impulses coming internationally.
But as I pointed to, we need to continue to strengthen our fiscal position. We’ve done that across a number of budgetsand we need to continue with productivity reforms.
Our inflation explorer tracks how prices have risen – or fallen – since 2022
Australia must navigate global factors in battle against inflation, assistant treasurer says
Higher-than-expected inflation figures and an increasingly likely rate rise are continuing to dominate the news cycle.
Asked why the government is unable to bring inflation down, the assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, pointed to the impact of international affairs on Australia’s economy.

double quotation markWhat we saw in the figures released earlier this week is that the conflict in Iran is lasting longer and is more severe than had been forecast, and that means that global energy prices are higher than had been expected a few months ago.
We’re seeing higher inflation than expected right across the advanced economy world.

Pushed on why other nations were having more success in bringing inflation down, Mulino said other countries “have not been anywhere near as successful as Australia in terms of their labour market outcomes”.
Thanks for taking us through those updates, Martin Farrer! I’ll steer us through the rest of the day’s news as we round off the last parliamentary sitting of the week.
Australia’s immediate neighbours are trusted more than historic allies, according to a new survey AAP reports on, which shows the United States is increasingly considered a “threat”.

Only half of the Australians polled in a YouGov survey, commissioned by the Australia Institute, considered longtime ally the US a “friend”. Meanwhile 42% perceived America as a “threat” (defined as a nation viewed with caution or suspicion).
Only 4% of young voters labelled the US a “close friend” while over half of young Australians considered it a threat.

Two-thirds of One Nation voters perceive the US as a friend, with the Coalition close behind. Labor voters are largely split and only one-quarter of Greens voters view the global superpower positively.

Only 21% of respondents had confidence in Donald Trump to “do the right thing” in world affairs, ahead of only the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un.
Indonesia, a close geographic neighbour and emerging partner, has been rated a more trusted partner than the United States, leading by 14% in the friend category.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says overheated discourse on social media is in large part responsible for the toxicity in politics, including the threats and abuse being sprayed at politicians.

Speaking at the Political Book of the Year awards in Canberra last night, Chalmers reflected on the alleged attack against Indi MP Helen Haines last week. He said hate had always been present in Australian society but it now has “a business model, a formula, an assembly line for mass-production.”
He described a new kind of digital misogyny that follows women in public life wherever they go, making the current climate harshest for women.

double quotation markThat climate is no accident. Hate is monetised and weaponised by algorithmic rage-bait. Extremism is incentivised; nuance is penalised. The most available public figures are the most vulnerable.
So tonight is a little reminder of why reason and research matters, why nuance matters, what’s at risk and what’s at stake and why that matters too.
Books inform our views without hardening them. Social media hardens our views without informing them.
Haines is recovering in hospital. Police have charged a 43-year-old man over the alleged attack outside her Wangaratta electorate office.
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Kat Wong with the main action.

items.title: Trump administration will allow pharmacies to make popular peptides
paragraphs: Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides. A new policy will make it easier for small compounding pharmacies to make them. Heather Diehl/Getty Images hide caption

Unproven but popular peptides touted for wellness have been available on the gray market, despite an official ban. Now, the Department of Health and Human Services is looking to bring them out of the shadows.
HHS said in a new policy that it will exercise enforcement discretion for a half dozen peptides, essentially looking the other way when they're made by small compounding pharmacies.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been a vocal supporter of peptides, saying he has used some of them himself.

Peptides are strings of amino acids, shorter than proteins, that can exert powerful effects in the body. Some occur naturally and others are synthetic variations. Wellness influencers and some clinicians have promoted unproven peptides for a wide range of uses, though the evidence for their safety and effectiveness is sparse.

So even though these peptides have not been through the Food and Drug Administration's rigorous drug review and approval process, they could become easier to get. But the policy's focus on smaller producers may mean that pharmacists will have a tough time meeting demand.

In July, a panel of advisers to the FDA voted in favor of expanded access to six peptides through compounding pharmacies. However, at the same meeting the FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the existing restrictions on them.
The new policy says compounding is a safer alternative to illicit "research-use-only" peptides that are available online. They're often sourced from sketchy suppliers overseas.
The peptides, and some of their unproven uses, are:

Joshua Fritzler, the president of Olympia and Wesley Pharmaceuticals in central Florida, says people have been asking about these peptides for years. But because they were illegal to compound, his company didn't make them.

The new policy doesn't change their legal status, but it does create a path for small compounders, called 503A compounding pharmacies. It doesn't apply to the larger ones, called 503Bs, that are outsourcing facilities producing higher volumes of medicines.
So at Fritzler's company, only its smaller compounding facility will be able to make the peptides – and only in small quantities, he says.

"We won't be able to meet demand," he says, explaining that Olympia will likely only compound one of the six peptides and needs to get its facility ready first. "I don't think all the [503]As in the country could meet the demand."

The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding's CEO Scott Brunner wrote in a statement that his group is pleased with the administration's decision to allow the peptides to be compounded because it offers a "more accountable alternative" for patients seeking gray market peptides.
"It also brings patients into a system where pharmacy standards, regulatory oversight, and serious adverse event reporting apply," he says.

Brunner warned, however, that it may take some time for compounding pharmacies to begin dispensing these products to patients. That's because ingredient suppliers need to make sure their active ingredients meet the policy's requirements — and pharmacies need to verify that, too.

Several consumer advocacy groups say the policy puts patients at risk, however. The nonprofit Public Citizen noted that Kennedy seems to have acted unilaterally rather than through the typical rulemaking process.

"By allowing unproven and potentially unsafe peptides to be manufactured, marketed and prescribed without concern about potential federal enforcement actions, Kennedy has undermined the FDA and threatened public health," Dr. Robert Steinbrook, Health Research Group Director at Public Citizen wrote in a statement. "All peptide substances should go through the standard FDA approval process for new drugs. The HHS Secretary should support, not sabotage, needed FDA enforcement actions to protect consumers."
Steinbrook advised clinicians to talk to their patients and tell them about the risk of contamination and other adverse effects.

The Partnership for Safe Medicines, which includes various pharmacy and pharmacist organizations around the country, filed a citizen petition last week, urging the FDA to ignore the recommendation from its advisory committee in July to allow compounding pharmacies to make the six peptides.

"Today's decision leaves Americans in a grey area as to whether peptides are safe or not, even though the FDA's own scientists recommended against voting in favor of these substances due to concerns with evidence," its executive director Shabbir Safda wrote in a statement.

items.title: Flávio Bolsonaro denies fleeing Brazil after landing in Miami
paragraphs: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who landed in Miami after losing the presidential election on Sunday, has said it was never his intention to "leave my homeland".
"I did not flee Brazil; I left for the sake of Brazil," he said in his first statement since leaving the country.
The US provided visas to him and his family, and on Wednesday US President Donald Trump told reporters: "We gave him a pass to come into the country".
Newly reelected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has criticised Bolsonaro's departure, saying "those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear".

Bolsonaro's arrival in Florida ended days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.

In a statement, distributed by the right-wing Brazilian influencer Paulo Figueiredo, Bolsonaro thanked both the presidents of Argentina and the US, and the American public "who share the same values ​​as the good people of my own country".
"It was never my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading," he said. "I departed from a regime of exception so that I could become the leader my people deserve."
He called himself a victim of a coup d'état and political persecution, and said his travel to the US was to protect his family.
He repeated unsubstantiated allegations of "electoral fraud" which he said allowed a "mathematical impossibility" to occur in the election.
On Wednesday, Trump declined to discuss the allegations made in Bolsonaro's letter.
"I won't get involved. It was a very strange election, that's for sure," Trump said. He went on to add that he thought Bolsonaro "and his family were treated very unfairly".

After Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil's election, Lula won the second round by more than four million votes, which was attributed to significantly higher turnout, and swaying more undecided voters.
The result was confirmed by the president of Brazil's top electoral court, himself appointed by his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.

Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.
For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday.
When he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.
With Bolsonaro's lawyers saying they did not know where he was, speculation quickly grew again that he might have left the country.

Hours later, however, Argentine migration authorities posted a tweet saying that Flávio Bolsonaro, his wife, and two daughters had only just crossed into Argentina over land on Tuesday night local time.
Flight tracking data verified by the BBC suggested the Bolsonaros departed from Puerto Iguazú in Argentina at 12:18 local time (03:18 GMT) on Wednesday to head to Guayaquil in Ecuador.
After a brief stop, the same private jet took them to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport, where they were pictured disembarking just before 09:30 local time (13:30 GMT).

Photographers, who had been waiting for his arrival to finally put an end to all the speculation, swarmed around Bolsonaro as he left the airport in Miami, while his team tried to cover him with umbrellas.
Flávio Bolsonaro is not the first member of his family to travel to the United States.
His father, Jair Bolsonaro, also left Brazil for Florida in December 2022 before his successor, Lula, was inaugurated.

Jair was still in the US when his supporters stormed Brazil's government buildings and Supreme Court on 8 January. He later used his absence as part of his defence in his coup trial, which led to a conviction and 27-year sentence.

Eduardo Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has been living in Texas after taking leave from Brazil's Congress. While in the US, he lobbied officials there in an attempt to influence the coup trial of his father, which led to the US imposing punitive tariffs on Brazil and sanctions on key officials.
Eduardo was convicted in absentia over this by Brazil's highest court earlier this year.
It is not yet clear what Flávio Bolsonaro's ultimate destination will be, nor how long he plans to stay in the US.
He is the subject of two investigations currently pending before Brazil's Supreme Federal Court.
One is regarding possible irregularities in the transfer of nearly $70m (£53m) from private bank Banco Master to the film Dark Horse – a biopic about his father.
The second investigation relates to alleged money laundering, both of which Bolsonaro denies.
He is set to lose his parliamentary immunity on 31 January, when his eight-year Senate term ends.

items.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
paragraphs: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses, and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work that they do for each agency.
Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted in leaks or hacks.
A representative of the DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was put online on Wednesday by a group called the Department of Peace alongside cybersecurity researcher and hacker maia crimew.
The information was put in a database named Icepick and shared through a website hosted by Distributed Denial of Secrets.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the goal of the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it's simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.
The Department of Peace said on Wednesday that it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.
Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.
A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."
Last month, the FBI was hacked with a group called ShinyHunters taking personal information about thousands of agents.
In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

items.title: Australian SAS officers knew about unlawful ‘throwdowns’ on dead Afghans, report says
paragraphs: Some Australian SAS officers knew that soldiers under their command were using “throwdowns” – planting weapons on dead Afghan civilians to portray them as combatants – but did nothing to stop the unlawful practice, a previously unpublished military report has said.

Posted online this week, the executive summary of a 2021 investigation into the “cultural context” of the special operations command by the inspector general of the Australian Defence Force (IGADF) is scathing about the “breakdown of command” and the erosion of military discipline during special forces operations in Afghanistan, which “resulted in episodes of potential and actual egregious behaviour”.

A previously published IGADF report, the Brereton Inquiry, made public in 2020, found credible information that Australian special forces personnel murdered 39 Afghan civilians and prisoners. But the Brereton report largely exonerated officers, saying the “criminal behaviour” it uncovered “was conceived, committed, continued, and concealed at patrol commander level”. Patrol commanders in the Australian SAS are not commissioned officers, they are typically corporals or sergeants.

However, the newly released report, commissioned after the Brereton findings by former defence force chief – and SAS officer – Angus Campbell in 2021, found some SAS officers knew about alleged “unlawful behaviour” and did not act to stop them.

“Officers with actual knowledge of misconduct in-theatre, including notably the use of throwdowns to effect in fraudulent reporting, or rumours of misconduct, did not take effective action to investigate and address these issues.”
The unlawful behaviour identified by the IGADF revealed “a breakdown of command” and ineffective leadership.

“The proper functioning of the ADF as a hierarchical system relies upon the enforcement of rules at all levels. A failure to do so has a corrosive effect on behaviours, morale and ultimately, military discipline, which in this case resulted in episodes of potential and actual egregious behaviour.”

SAS officers allowed the regiment to develop an “uncontrolled ‘warrior’ ethos” and the long, grinding, nature of the Afghan conflict, to which a small cohort of SAS soldiers were repeatedly sent on dangerous, corrosive deployments, contributed to moral injury and impaired decision-making.
“The group dynamic within a special forces deployment influences the shift in moral compass of some individuals,” the report said.
“The incremental shift in moral compass in response to violence, killing, morally questionable decisions and unconventional features, can create moral injury.”

The report found that the excessively secretive and insular nature of the SAS also contributed to worsening standards as did an “inversion” of the chain of command, where senior non-commissioned officers were able to dominate officers who were, ostensibly, their superiors.
“This resulted in junior officers being effectively subservient to non-commissioned officers, and occupying a position which can best be described as ‘learned helplessness’.”

The report cited the fact SAS soldiers were consistently allowed to drink alcohol while on deployment in Afghanistan – in defiance of orders imposed on others – “sent the strong signal to those involved that the rules did not apply to them”.
The use of “throwdowns” was a known breach that officers failed to stop.

“The unwillingness to challenge non-commissioned officers was particularly apparent from the breakdown of military discipline through a lack of proper supervision. The failure to address the widely known use of throwdowns is an example of this.
“This was also a manifestation of a broader breakdown of military discipline within the SAS regiment. The tolerance of officers of overt non-compliance sent a powerful signal.”

Similarly, soldiers wrote false reports of their actions on the battlefield, focused on rules of engagement and laced with circumlocution, which “assisted perpetrators of misconduct to conceal their actions”.

“A particular manifestation was the use of variations of a standard phrase ‘manoeuvring to a position of tactical advantage’, to describe the actions of civilian ‘squirters’ as direct participants in hostilities, which justified engagement … under the rules of engagement. The expression was used with such regularity that it lost meaning.”

The report’s executive summary says there was “a significant failure of good leadership and effective command” across the SAS commanders, and that the reporting systems designed to prevent misconduct had become “depleted and largely unreliable”, giving officers “a false level of assurance”.
“The culture of the Special Operations Task Group … was not the cause of misconduct but created an environment which enabled misconduct by a few to occur.”
Defence had previously refused to release the report despite it being the subject of freedom of information requests and an attempt to force its disclosure in the Senate.

items.title: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
paragraphs: Protecting this region from climate change is a theme of the King's trip and was the focus of his visit to the Bonefish Pond National Park. The site was once a rubbish dump but has been redeveloped and now protects 1,235 acres of mangroves.
The King walked along a new boardwalk through the wetlands to see the conservation work being done to protect this vulnerable, low lying island from climate change.
He met students carrying out field work in the wetland waters asking them about their exams and ambitions to be marine biologists.
"We've so been looking forward to this," said Joanne Smith, President of the Bahamas National Trust Council.
"We want more Bahamians to get involved in our national parks so they can use it to better themselves… we are so pleased to have the King here, this is really significant for us."
Then it was on to the Junkanoo, where the King could be seen dancing alongside attendees dressed in feathered headdresses and bright costumes.
The history of the Junkanoo is not clear but it's believed it emerged out of the slave trade when enslaved men and women were given time off to mark Christmas.
A small protest near the parade was moved on by the police.
The King ended his day with a garden reception at Government House in Nassau where he met Bahamians who have made significant contributions to public life.

In a speech, Dame Cynthia A Pratt, the governor general of the Bahamas who is the King's representative on the island, described her pride at Charles visiting the country for the first time since 1973.
"We trust that your time in our capital will reflect the legendary hospitality of our people," said Dame Cynthia.
"We pray that this royal visit further strengthens the enduring bonds of friendship between the Crown and the Bahamian people."
On Thursday, the Caribbean tour leaves the Bahamas as the King continues his visit in Guyana.

The trip has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.
The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity.
He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.
The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

items.title: A hacker stole more than 40,000 DHS employee records
paragraphs: is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

A hacker stole a trove of personal information from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The breach exposes the names, job titles, phone numbers, email addresses, and office locations of more than 41,000 employees, including those in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), according to TechCrunch and Wired. The data also linked the agencies to specific surveillance tools.

As reported by TechCrunch, a hacker known as “Department of Peace” gained access to the data through Okta, an identity and access management service used by the DHS. Around 21,000 records pertain to CBP employees, and nearly 7,000 belong to staff at ICE. The data also includes records from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI).

The DHS has worked to conceal the identities of CBP and ICE agents, who have carried out anti-immigration raids around the US, while also tracking down online critics. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” the “Department of Peace” hacker said, according to TechCrunch. This leak comes just weeks after hackers stole data from the FBI on its employees and job applicants.

The leaked DHS information was reportedly given to cybersecurity researcher maia arson crimew, who shared it with Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a nonprofit organization that’s now hosting the leaked “Icepick” dataset. The leak also reportedly includes information about DHS groups that have access to tools that can be used for surveillance, such as the facial recognition app Mobile Fortify and PenLink, which can collect and analyze data from phones and online services.
The DHS didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

items.title: Brazilian political drama unfolds as defeated Flavio Bolsonaro arrives in Miami
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6020518/nx-s1-9982746" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">

Defeated presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro and his family have arrived in the U.S. after Brazilian authorities ordered him to surrender his passport. He is facing multiple investigations in Brazil.

This morning, Brazilians were glued to their screens watching a private plane land at an airport in Miami, Florida. Moments later, the man who had just lost Brazil's presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro, stepped out onto the tarmac. His arrival capped three days of political drama since his stunning defeat to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. NPR South America correspondent Carrie Kahn is on the line now. Hey, Carrie.
SUMMERS: So, Carrie, I want to make sure I understand this correctly. Bolsonaro lost Sunday's election, and by Wednesday, he was in the U.S.?

KAHN: Yes, it's been a wild ride the past three days. On Sunday, he refused to concede the election and said he would petition to annul the results. The next day, his party did accept the results. And in a video, Bolsonaro seemed to back down a bit but added that federal police demanded his passport after he was visiting his father, who is under house arrest for attempting to overturn his own electoral loss to Lula four years ago. By Tuesday - yesterday - rumors were flying that Bolsonaro had fled Brazil, and today he arrived in Miami and then later put out a statement first declaring himself as, quote, "the true elected president of Brazil." Then a bit later, he posted a new statement downgrading himself to the true elected leader of Brazil. He compared himself to liberation figures like Charles de Gaulle and María Corina Machado of Venezuela, amongst others.
SUMMERS: Interesting. OK, lots of questions here. One is this - do we know how he managed to leave Brazil and get to the U.S.?

KAHN: Argentine officials reported he crossed into the country last night, but Brazilian officials say they have no record of him crossing. Bolsonaro also has an Italian passport. From Argentina, he flew to Ecuador and then on to Miami. And in his letter today, he thanked Argentina's president, Javier Milei, for his support. And Milei is a far-right ally of Bolsonaro and Trump. And like Trump, Milei has still not recognized Brazil's election results. Trump was asked just a little while ago what he thought of Bolsonaro declaring himself leader of Brazil. Trump said he wasn't going to comment on that.
SUMMERS: Got it. Why did Brazil's federal police revoke his passport?

KAHN: That order came from a Supreme Court justice who said Bolsonaro was a flight risk because he's facing several investigations, and that justice oversaw the case against Bolsonaro's father, Jair. In his letter today, Flávio said that Brazil's judiciary has been, quote, "weaponized" against his entire family. The cases against Bolsonaro include a money laundering scheme tied to online gambling. Another involves questionable financing of a biopic about his father. Bolsonaro denies any wrongdoing.
SUMMERS: And people in Brazil, what have they had to say about his sudden departure?

KAHN: As you can imagine, the country has been captivated. You know, look, the election was decisive for Lula, but nearly 60 million people voted for Bolsonaro and his conservative movement. I spoke with Fábio Zanini, a political columnist with Folha, a newspaper in São Paulo, who says Flávio's departure could help that movement.

FÁBIO ZANINI: Flávio will be in the United States now, close to the Trump administration, attacking Brazil, saying that he's a persecuted person and trying to portray himself as a victim of Brazilian persecution. That might give a new energy to the Bolsonarista movement.

KAHN: Many also say that claims of election tampering and political persecution are pretty hollow because Bolsonaro's party did make huge gains throughout the country. His stepmother and his brother were elected senators, and the party has now the largest majority in Congress.

items.title: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
paragraphs: A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.

It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.
The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the crash, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.
Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.
The crash happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.
The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said.

He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.
The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.
Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."
One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.
Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.
Spanish journalist Antonio Jiménez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened.
"I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described.
"I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."
Another passenger, 46-year-old Sebastián Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms."
"It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.
Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms.
"She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.
Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.
Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims.
"The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."
Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near Córdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.
Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain.
"Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the the main opposition People's Party.
Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".
Sánchez and other Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

items.title: Mbappé, Real Madrid forced to apologize over 'dictator' comment about China's Mao Zedong
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.
France and Real Madrid soccer star Kylian Mbappé is facing a backlash in China after commercial sponsors cut ties with him over comments he made about China's founding leader Mao Zedong.
In a recent interview Mbappé described finding a meme—which photoshopped him onto an image resembling that of Mao and referred to it as a "Chinese dictator."
Mbappé has since issued a public apology for his comments as Chinese brands dropped Mbappe and a broadcaster suspended broadcasting Spain's La Liga matches.

In an apology issued on Tuesday in both Chinese and French, Mbappé said that his comment during a recent interview was “ill-judged”, adding that he now understands that it hurt "many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world."
A U.S. congressional committee on China said Mbappé should not have apologized for calling Mao Zedong a "dictator."

The U.S. House Select Committee on China posted a statement on X, saying that Mao Zedong "was indeed a dictator, and the harm he inflicted upon the Chinese people was far more severe than anything a soccer player might say."

The committee, chaired by Congressman John Moolenaar (R-MI), followed up with a repost of a video it recently created about the Cultural Revolution, which Mao launched 60 years ago, calling it “one of the darkest chapters in Chinese history”.
Former Turkish American basketball player and rights activist Enes Kanter Freedom also suggested he disagreed with Mbappe's apology.

“I'm not here to judge Mbappe for apologizing. I don't know what pressure he faced,” Freedom told VOA Tuesday. “But you know, when athletes feel they have to choose between their principles and their careers, we have a serious problem. So that's why I think it's a shame that he came out and apologized because Mao Zedong is a dictator.”

A video clip from an interview with Mbappé on the French show The Bridge has been circulating on social media platforms since Monday. When asked which meme featuring his likeness is the funniest, Mbappé mentioned one where his face is superimposed onto an image of a "Chinese dictator."

Mbappé did not name the character by name, but the show’s post-production team inserted an image of his face superimposed onto a portrait of Mao, implying that he was referring to Mao, triggering the backlash in China.

The following day, several Chinese enterprises—including beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu, and cheese maker Milkground, moved to terminate all partnerships with Mbappé, saying they had "zero-tolerance" policy toward "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people". The official China Central Television (CCTV) began suspending all broadcasts related to the Spanish football league LALIGA and matches involving Mbappé, and all advertisements featuring him have been pulled.

Mbappé, the 2026 World Cup Golden Boot winner currently plays for Real Madrid in Spain. He helped France win the 2018 World Cup and scored a hattrick in the 2022 World Cup final. Mbappé is considered one of the most influential and commercially valuable soccer players in the world today. Until this week's incident, he had multiple lucrative sponsorship deals with Chinese companies.
Spain's premier league football known as La Liga has issued an official apology to China over Mbappé’s comment on Tuesday. Real Madrid issued a similar apology Wednesday.
Asked about Mbappe's apology during a regular press briefing in Beijing Wednesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: "We take seriously the apology that the person has made."

Mao Zedong who led China from 1949 until his death in 1976 is revered in China as the “Great Leader” and the main founder of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the People’s Republic China. In the 1980’s, Chinese authorities, in their attempt to launch reforms and break away from the Cultural Revolution era, once acknowledged some “serious mistakes” made by Mao. However, the current leader Xi Jinping has publicly expressed his admiration for Mao and called him a "great patriot and national hero of China in modern times."

Mao’s critics in China and abroad view him as one of the deadliest dictators in human history. In its X post, the U.S. House Select Committee on China alleged that Mao's "dictatorship and disastrous policies killed tens of millions of Chinese people in the Cultural Revolution, the Great Famine, and other atrocities.”

The committee’s post added: “The real disgrace in this news story is the companies rushing to apologize so they can continue to do business in China. The CCP is the largest oppressor of the Chinese people and their human rights, and those businesses that work with the CCP help normalize its crushing brutality.”
Mbappé is not the first sports figure to face varying degrees of censorship or boycotts in China due to their public comments.

Ironically, it was a former Real Madrid and Arsenal star, Mesut Özil who, through social media post, criticized Chinese government policies and the detention of Uyghurs in Xinjiang in December 2019. Özil left Arsenal in 2021 to joint Turkish club Fenerbahçe though it's unclear whether it was related to the comments he made about China.

Freedom himself faced similar problems when he criticized Chinse communist party in October 2021. After making remarks on social media and during games that were critical of Chinese actions in Tibet, Xinjiang, and Taiwan, broadcasts of games featuring his then-team, the Boston Celtics, were halted in China. Chinse platforms such as Tencent Sports also scrubbed all videos and merchandise related to him.

Chinese companies also suspended broadcasting NBA games after two NBA-related incidents involving the former General Manager of the NBA’s Houston Rockets, Daryl Morey, and former LA Lakers star Dwight Howard in 2019 and in 2023. The suspensions cost the NBA millions of dollars in revenue from broadcasting rights.
VOA Mandarin’s Stella Hsu contributed to this article.

items.title: Akai is embracing vibe-coded mods with an open-source MPC
paragraphs: is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The MPC Sample Key isn’t even formally announced yet, but Akai is already showing off what the modding community is cooking up through vibe coding. Akai has decided to embrace the explosion of hackers and custom firmware developers by giving them early access to the device, which will have open-source firmware.

It will likely run some version of the same software found on the MPC Sample, but with tweaks to accommodate the traditional keyboard, pitch, and mod wheels. Unlike the higher-end MPC Key 37, however, the Sample Key doesn’t have pads. Instead, you play back samples with the keys.

In the short Instagram Reels posted last night and today, Akai shows a number of vibe-coded mods that add synths, including Native Instruments Massive, to the device, as well as virtual analog and FM synths. One is even shown running a completely custom OS, with “several different synths in it.”

According to the clips, the same “community” features will come to the regular MPC Sample, which is also shown running a few vibe-coded synths built by Claude. That could mean Akai plans to open-source the entire MPC Sample platform.

CEO Jack O’Donnell told The Verge that inMusic brands, especially Akai, would be looking to embrace the modding community by seeding early devices to developers. These efforts will also include open-sourcing some software and providing an SDK.

items.title: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks
paragraphs: The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between members states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.

A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.

The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.
The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.
It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.

But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.
Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.

Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.

At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.
Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.

“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.

Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.

Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he ​interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.

A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.
Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.

Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about ⁠specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will ​make to the lives ​of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement ​had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, ​including an acknowledgment that ‌defining the ​term would take ​another year.

items.title: Former Russian detainee’s sister says Stephen Hubbard ‘escaped hell’
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

The sister of former Russian detainee Stephen Hubbard says her brother's condition is better than the family expected. The 74-year-old American was released from Russia after more than four years in detention and returned to the United States last week.

"It was incredible. I don’t even know how to describe it. It’s simply unbelievable to realize that he is free and has escaped the hell he spent nearly five years in," his sister, Patricia Hubbard, said in a recent interview with VOA.
"He underwent all the examinations and tests. Now he needs to rebuild his muscles and regain his strength," she said.

Russian forces detained Stephen Hubbard in the Russian occupied-Ukrainian town of Izium in April of 2022, where he had lived and taught English since 2014. Russia convicted him of being a mercenary and sentenced him to six to 10 years in a penal colony in October of 2024. Patricia Hubbard says her brother was never a mercenary.
"That was just a pretext to take his property," she told VOA, adding that her brother had absolutely no intention of joining the Ukrainian military or taking part in the Russia-Ukraine war.

"He hated the war. He was against it. Stephen was never a military man. Yes, he served in the U.S. Air Force, but that was not during wartime," she said. "As a child, he never got into fights. He wasn’t one of those boys who was always getting into trouble. He was a good, quiet child who took part in the [Boy] Scouts and read a great deal. He always loved books."
Patricia Hubbard told VOA that she heard of her brother's possible release about two days before it happened.

"I was told that everything could change at the last minute," she said. "They [U.S. officials] did say, expect anything to happen at the last minute because that's happened before when a country will say they're going to let someone out, then they like to torture you by not letting them out [until the] last minute."
She noted that the moment she saw her brother was special.
"We just hugged. We kept telling each other, “I love you,” over and over again. We hugged for a long time," Patricia Hubbard said.

Stephen Hubbard spent the first days in the U.S. under medical evaluation. His sister says after a medical assessment, he was sent home with a new set of clothes, new medical records, a new passport, and identification.
"When someone is taken hostage, they lose everything. Everything is stripped from them," she told VOA.
Patricia, who holds a master's in psychological counseling, said she chose not to talk to her brother about his experience in the Russian jail, where she said he was tortured.
"Some of the guards who knew only a few words in English would shout, 'Die, American, die!' while beating him," she said.

"Psychologically, he is doing much better than expected," Hubbard said. "His faith has helped him enormously. Psychologically, he has been through a great deal. But he did say one thing. He said, 'I want to be around people I know and who love me.' He said there is no love in that place. No love at all. Only darkness."
While in the Russian jail, Patricia says her brother Stephen spent most of his time in complete isolation.

"And even when someone else was nearby, they didn’t speak the same language," she told VOA. "There was no television or radio. He had no sense of time. He had absolutely no idea how much the world had changed over the past five years. All of it is a shock to him. It’s as if you had fallen into a coma and then woken up.”

items.title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
paragraphs: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.
The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36.
Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment.
"Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.
Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

items.title: Readwise is taking on Kindle and Kobo for ebook supremacy
paragraphs: For the last several years, Readwise has been building tools for power readers. There’s the eponymous product, Readwise, which stores and categorizes your Kindle highlights to help you remember what you’ve read. There’s Readwise Reader, an app for reading newsletters, PDFs, and web articles you’ve saved for later. And now there’s Readwise Books, a full-fledged platform for buying, reading, and talking about books.

Readwise Books is currently in beta, available through invite or to existing Readwise subscribers. I’ve been testing the app for a few days, and it’s a much bigger take on reading than most. Tristan Homsi and Daniel Doyon, Readwise’s cofounders, like to call the platform “Strava for reading” because it can track how long, how much, and how fast you read, and it can show that information to friends you make in the Readwise Books app. The app’s homepage is a feed of what other people are reading, with comments and recommendations laced throughout.

“Strava for reading” wasn’t the original goal of Readwise Books, which has been part of the Readwise plan since the beginning. “Literally, Dan and I talked about this when we first met,” Homsi says. “We feel like Kindle could be so much better. We really didn’t think it would take nine-plus years to be able to get to this point.” But it turns out, Doyon adds, that for all their ideas about innovation in books, “no one sits around wanting a better Kindle.” But there is one thing they do wish for: a better Goodreads. “Everybody hates Goodreads.”

In a sense, then, the plan for Readwise Books is to take on Kindle by first taking on Goodreads. The Readwise Books app offers a nice way to track books you want to read, are reading, and have read; it even syncs with your Kindle account to let you track books you’ve bought from Amazon by taking pictures of your starting and ending pages. You can rate and review books and see what others have said. It’s a little Strava, a little Letterboxd, and a lot nicer to look at than Goodreads.

The long-term goal, of course, is to get people to stop buying Kindle books and start buying from Readwise. Homsi and Doyon have spent the last several years working to reach deals with all five of the major US publishers in order to have a competitive library of books available. That meant endless negotiations, security reviews, DRM debates, and more — both cofounders seem exhausted just talking about the process. But eventually, by several small miracles, they got the deals done. And since those deals govern the price of books, and many things about how they’re sold and presented, they bring Readwise to a nearly even playing field almost immediately.

It all took a lot longer than expected, but Doyon and Homsi think their timing might actually be pretty good. Digital book reading continues to grow, particularly among young people; a huge amount of that reading happens on phones and tablets. Meanwhile, a new crop of E Ink devices like the tiny Xteink and the Boox Palma line have expanded the universe of available hardware for a company like Readwise.

Not long ago, Doyon says, they would have had no choice but to build an e-reader of their own. (And he says they still might.) Now, they can just make sure it runs on an E Ink-friendly flavor of Android.

After a couple of days using Readwise Books, I can say confidently I already like it better than practically all of its competition. It’s a much nicer-looking app than anything you’ll get from Kindle or Kobo; it has lots of ways to customize how books look; and at least for now, I’m finding the tracking features compel me to read more instead of annoying me. (Homsi says some early versions of the gamification features were substantially more annoying.) I’ve found a few bugs, and the half-integration with Kindle is a little confusing in spots, but it’s already a really nice place to read.

Of course, I, like millions of other people, already own a Kindle and lots of Kindle books. Switching ebook platforms is hard, and Doyon says he’s not counting on everyone to do it right away. He says he’s hopeful Readwise can persuade existing users to switch, in order to sync their notes and progress more seamlessly. He’s also hoping that the advent of AI, and the ways in which AI reliance may rot our brains, will get a lot of people back into the idea of reading more deeply again. And that a bunch of those people might be looking for a nicer, more social place to do so.
