items.title: What's gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving
paragraphs: Cookie Jones, left, quit her job to provide care to her mother who has Alzheimer's disease. Caregivers often earn less as they take time off work to help aging family members. Tyler Russell/Connecticut Public via Getty Images hide caption
Tyler Russell/Connecticut Public via Getty Images

As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP and shared first with NPR, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average.
The increase during those years is more than twice the overall rate of inflation of 24%, as measured by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index.
What's driving the ramp-up? Food, housing and medical expenses are the biggest chunk, finds the study, which queried 2,538 family caregivers.

The bump in costs comes as family caregivers take on more care and more complicated medical responsibilities at home, says Megan O'Reilly, vice president of governmental affairs at AARP. "The more care that's needed, the more it costs."

And increased spending is only part of the story. The demands of caregiving often require people to reduce their working hours or quit work entirely, the survey finds. It's a double whammy: increased costs on top of lost income.

Meghan Maher has seen that first-hand. Just seven weeks after the birth of her first baby, her mother was diagnosed with advanced cancer. Suddenly, Maher was a "sandwich" caregiver — parent and child needing her at the same time.
Meghan Maher and her mom Connie Cadwell. In order to help her mother through cancer treatment and care for her young children, Maher had to leave her career. Maher family hide caption
At first, she tried to manage it all. She returned to her career in cancer research after maternity leave, but keeping up with the demands of work, her mom and her newborn son was too much.
She shrank her hours to part time. But even that wasn't manageable. There was no way to attend all her mother's appointments, coordinate her care, and also be available for big deadlines on the job.

She quit, and the family's income fell by half. Because her husband had a good job, they weren't struggling, but "it was definitely scary," she says now. As her mom got sicker her parents moved in, increasing the household expenses.

Soon after her mother's death in 2017, her father had a series of major complications from abdominal surgery and was critically ill for months. Maher needed to be by his side during hospital stays, advocating for him on a moment's notice, so now the family also needed to pay for child care. She estimates the cost at about $10,000 a year.
Her father eventually recovered, and the family was able to manage despite the difficulties. Many aren't so lucky.

About half of all family caregivers say they've made major financial sacrifices, according to the AARP report: Working more hours, cutting savings, or even drawing down on money put away for retirement.

Many Americans deal with the cost of care, and more will in the future. About 63 million people now provide ongoing help for a family member or friend — roughly 1 in 4 adults. The need will likely grow: An estimated 70 percent of the people turning 65 today will need some form of help as they age.

Medicare does not pay for routine help either at home or in a facility, and that care is expensive. In 2025, 40 hours of in-home caregiving help a week ran about $72,792 a year, according to the insurance company Genworth, which conducts annual surveys of the cost of care. Skilled nursing costs an average of $115,000 per year for a shared room.

When Maher returned to work, she became a professional death doula. That means she helps clients with the emotional and practical challenges at the end of life. She's self-employed, so she can control her own schedule and limit the number of clients she serves. It allows her the flexibility to help her father as he ages. But her income is half what it would have been in her old career.

With the clients she helps, she sees other ways that care costs pile up. In Florida where she lives, it's routine for chronically ill people to hire an attorney in order to qualify for Medicaid, which unlike Medicare does foot the bill for long-term care. Even though they are eligible for the benefits, the paperwork is so complex that they wind up paying for legal help to navigate it. In Florida, she says, that runs about $6,000.

What she has seen and experienced motivates her to call attention to the caregiving crunch. In May, Maher testified before Congress at a special Senate committee on aging. "Caregiving has also reshaped my professional life," she said to the Senate committee. "The flexibility of self-employment comes with real financial and professional tradeoffs." She was invited by Daughterhood, an organization that offers support and resources for caregivers.

Family caregivers can access some public money, depending on where they live. All states pay some types of family caregivers through Medicaid. In California, for instance, more than 800,000 caregivers earn between $16.90 and $25 an hour for in-home work. Funds for these programs are likely to dwindle due to President Trump's big budget bill that cut nearly $1 trillion out of Medicaid funding over the next decade.

If the person who needs care is eligible for Veterans Administration benefits, they may also be entitled to financial help to cover the cost of caregiving. Like Medicaid, the rules are complex, and many family caregivers hire advocates to advise on eligibility and the application procedure.

The cost of care hasn't been as visible as the cost of gasoline, food and healthcare, says AARP executive vice president Nancy LeaMond. She believes that will change. "When you see the number of people paying this kind of money, I think that'll be an impetus for action in the legislative arena."

In the last few years, Congress has introduced various proposals that could put some money back into the pockets of caregivers, such as allowing caregivers to spend money from their tax-sheltered health savings accounts on their parents' medical expenses. In some states, new rules are already a reality.

Six states now offer tax credits to family caregivers for expenses like retrofitting a home with grab bars or railings, usually between $1,000 and $5,000 a year. Two other states have more limited programs. Last year, two U.S. Senators introduced a bipartisan bill that would establish a similar $5,000 tax credit nationwide.

In 14 states and the District of Columbia, most employers are required to offer paid family and medical leave. Those policies include time off for caregiving for a family member. Another bill introduced into Congress would convert that into a national policy that would require up to 12 weeks of partly paid leave for some workers.

A third proposed federal law would protect the Social Security benefits of caregivers. Under current rules, a person who stops working in order to care full-time for family sees their future Social Security check shrink, because they are no longer earning credits toward retirement. This bill would change the law to continue awarding points to full-time caregivers.

"We spend a lot of time talking to members of Congress, and you can't raise this issue in a meeting without being interrupted by someone telling their own story," says LeaMond. "In time, I believe that will coalesce to support family caregiving."
Kat McGowan is an independent journalist covering adult caregiving who reports the series "What It Takes" for NPR.

items.title: US official to VOA on Iranian regime: 'Unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.
A senior American official has reiterated President Donald Trump's recent threats to resume military action against Iran's Islamic regime if refuses to stop its threatening activities.

"Unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job," the official told VOA on background in a Monday email. The official was responding to a request for comment on the Iranian regime hosting a meeting earlier in the day with senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye.

Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Head of Turkish Intelligence Ibrahim Kalin arrived in Tehran on Monday and met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
There were no immediate readouts of the talks from Riyadh, Islamabad or Ankara, three nations that formed a mutual defense alliance known as the Mecca Agreement in August.

Ahead of the Tehran meeting, a statement from the Saudi foreign ministry said it was part of an effort by the Mecca Agreement countries to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis, encourage dialogue and diplomatic solutions, and support mediation efforts of Qatar and Pakistan."

The U.S. launched a joint offensive with Israel against the Iranian terror regime on February 28, severely damaging its nuclear weaponization program and other malign capabilities. Major combat ended with a Qatar- and Pakistan-mediated April truce that has largely held, with the U.S. carrying out several rounds of retaliatory strikes for Iranian attacks that violated the ceasefire.
The intense period of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran also saw the regime retaliate with aerial attacks on America's regional Arab partners including Saudi Arabia.

The U.S. official who provided the background comment to VOA said Trump “holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States." Describing the Islamic republic as a "failed country," the official added: "The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing."
The official noted that "crushing" U.S. sanctions and naval blockades that have prevented Tehran from exporting its oil have crippled Iran’s economy and left it "completely broke."
"Iran has been decimated, and one way or the other, the conflict in Iran will be over very soon," the official said.

Referring to the Iranian regime, the official further added: "Their military was decimated by Operation Epic Fury, and they are unable to pay their troops. The Hormuz Strait is open and tens of millions of barrels of oil are escorted out of the Strait every day."

The Iranian regime has warned against an escalation of the conflict and threatened to widen hostilities if attacked again. In an opinion piece in the Financial Times last week, Araghchi also said his country was ready for diplomatic resolution.
President Trump told reporters last Wednesday that he was not negotiating with Iran and predicted that a new Iran-related development will happen "fairly soon."

items.title: Australia must recruit hundreds more to crew Aukus submarines, retired admiral warns
paragraphs: Australia faces an uphill battle to recruit and train enough naval personnel to serve on submarines planned for the future fleet of nuclear-powered vessels under the controversial $368bn Aukus deal, a retired admiral has warned.

As the Virginia-class submarine USS Colorado arrived at HMAS Stirling south of Perth on Tuesday for a month of routine maintenance and to help build Australian expertise, retired admiral Peter Briggs said more people needed to be enrolled in the navy’s submarine program.

As part of a $368bn trilateral defence deal, Australia will acquire between three and five Virginia-class, nuclear-powered submarines from the United States to replace its five diesel-electric Collins-class vessels, which are becoming obsolete.
The new submarines are much bigger and require up to 134 crew – almost three times the number needed for the Collins class.
The Royal Australian Navy says it has 230 personnel in various stage of the US nuclear-powered submarine training pipeline.

“Of these, approximately 145 have completed US Naval nuclear power training and are now building experience training on US Navy SSNs [a hull classification for nuclear-powered submarines],” a navy spokesperson said.
“By 2030, we expect to have 400 Royal Australian Navy officers and sailors trained and ready to serve.”
But Briggs urged a more intensive recruitment plan to crew the bigger boats.
“We have got to triple the size of the submarine arm and we’ve got to train them in nuclear skills,” he said.
“You are heading toward needing a submarine arm of 3,000, that’s the hill you have to climb.”
Approximately 850 submariners are qualified to operate Collins-class vessels.
The Virginia-class boats are intended to bridge the transition from the Collins-class fleet to the future SSN-AUKUS submarine, an even bigger design being developed by Australia and the UK.
“The personnel side is a huge issue, but it’s not the only one,” Briggs said.
The former submariner argued that maintaining two different submarine types would add complexity to training, logistics, maintenance and spare-parts arrangements.
The Australian government did not respond to questions about recruitment targets and whether a workforce development program was on track.
Recruitment is further complicated by the need for more than a dozen different trades, from radio and sonar operators to cooks and electricians.

After spending the next month is Perth, the USS Colorado will return to the city’s waters again in late 2027 as part of the Submarine Rotational Force-West program which is designed to help Australia build the skills and infrastructure to operate its own nuclear fleet.
From 2027, the program will see up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarine rotate through HMAS Stirling.

Paul Johnson, HMAS Stirling fleet base west commodore, said the USS Colorado maintenance period would be used to “practise and test our procedures across a range of nuclear-related operational scenarios”.
Officials stressed that no radiological material would be transferred during the maintenance period and that nuclear-related exercises would be simulated.
Late last year, Senate estimates heard that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could rotate through Australian ports despite a non-proliferation commitment.
USS Colorado captain, Justin Reeves, said the US government would not “confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on specific platforms”.
Colorado was built in 2018 and arrived this week carrying conventional weapons, including four torpedoes and four “payload tubes” that can be used to house and launch weapons.

It took two weeks to travel to Perth from Pearl Harbor in Hawaii with 160 men and no women aboard. A sign labelled “Berth Rules”, taped to the wall near the submarine’s entryway, listed “Don’t be stinky” as the crew’s top priority once they reach port.
The demands of living and working in confined spaces for extended periods presents another recruitment challenge for officials.
Sleeping arrangements can involve bunks stacked three high, while “hot racking” allows three sailors to share two beds by rotating their sleeping schedules around watch duties.
In some circumstances, and when accommodation is limited, sailors may sleep in torpedo rooms.
Reeves said the vessel is “built for combat, not for comfort”.
Nuclear submarines don’t need to refuel, meaning their range is effectively infinite. “The limits of its endurance are really food and toilet paper, and that’s several months’ worth,” Reeves said.
“Being nuclear powered is a massive advantage.”

items.title: Russell Brand tells court allegations had devastating impact on him
paragraphs: Russell Brand has said a documentary that made allegations about his behaviour had a "devastating" effect on him, and made friends and colleagues turn against him.
The entertainer has begun giving evidence as his defence case gets under way at his trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.
Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.
Asked whether consent was important to him, he told the court: "Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed many ways more important than sex itself."
After Brand entered the witness box on Wednesday morning, defence barrister Ian Winter KC began by taking him through the indictment, asking him if he had committed the offences.
After each question, Brand replied "no" loudly towards the jury.
Brand was then asked about a documentary that aired in 2023, which included some allegations against him.
Asked by Winter what impact the documentary had had on his friends and colleagues turning their backs on him, Brand said: "It was devastating."
Winter questioned whether Brand had been able to persuade any friend or acquaintance who might have been able to give evidence on his behalf to appear in court.
Brand, wearing a black suit with an open neck white shirt and a loose black tie, replied: "I have not."
Winter asked: "Will they touch you with a bargepole?" Brand said: "No."

Brand also claimed in court that he was told he could not stay with his son at Great Ormond Street hospital in London when the child was having open heart surgery, following the documentary and a newspaper investigation.
He told the court: "Due to material that had been published in the public eye they had to bar my attendance and presence.
"They were unclear about what legal reason there was but that was the reason they gave to my wife Laura and I."
Brand told the court: "My entire life has been consumed by these allegations," adding that he had "devoted myself to these matters".
Winter asked Brand if he recalled meeting the first complainant, who alleges he raped her at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.
Brand said yes, explaining that he found her "loquacious" and "interesting".
When asked if there was any truth in the allegations that he raped her, he said: "No."
Brand was then asked about another woman, who alleges that the entertainer grabbed her breasts before dragging her into a toilet and raping her.

Brand said he recalled been invited to a party in London at a bar in 2004, and said a friend had introduced him to the complainant by saying "something like 'there's a bird here who really wants to meet you mate'."
When asked if he remembered what he said to her upon meeting, he told the court: "I would have said something like, 'You're really, really beautiful'."
The barrister asked whether he had grabbed her breasts. "Absolutely not," Brand replied.
When questioned if he would have behaved in the way that had been alleged, he said it would have amounted to "disgusting behaviour".
"I was increasingly focused on my promiscuity," he said. "That's not the way I would have behaved because it's not only criminal but vulgar."
Brand said he remembered going into the toilet with her but said "no" when asked if he had dragged or forced her there.
"Did your penis enter her mouth at all whilst in the cubicle?" Winter asked. "No," said Brand.
Another complainant, who worked at MTV, alleges that Brand tried to drag her into a toilet at work in 2001.
At the time, he was one of the channel's star presenters. She said she managed to wrench herself away.
Asked if he had intended a non-consensual sexual encounter, Brand told the court: "Absolutely not."
Brand was also asked about his wedding to singer Katy Perry in October 2010 and whether it brought a "sea change" to his life. He said the marriage brought him "staggering fame".
Being cross examined later, Brand agreed with the prosecution's suggestion that he blamed Channel 4 documentary programme Dispatches for the allegations.
Asked if the media had been fair to him, Brand said he "would reject that suggestion strongly".

items.title: At least 31 dead and 80 injured after two trains collide in Spain – latest updates
paragraphs: The death toll from today’s train collision has risen to 31, according to the latest information from local government in Castile-La Mancha.
All Spanish Cup football games cancelled as mark of respect
EU 'ready to support' Spanish investigation into train crash
At least 30 dead, 80 injured, with concerns death toll could rise further - what we know
Aerial footage from the crash scene - video
At least 30 dead, 80 injured, but numbers likely to rise, local president says
Death toll may rise further, local government spokesperson warns
At least 30 dead in Spanish train crash, local government confirms
Spanish royals express concern for and support to all affected by train crash
'Europe mourns in you,' EU's von der Leyen responds to train collision in Spain
At least 30 dead after two train collide in Spain - what do we know
Spain's transport minister working to 'obtain all possible information'
Spanish PM, opposition leader 'shocked' by train crash in Toledo
Spanish health minister fears 'major tragedy' after train collision in Toledo
Toledo crash brings back memories of deadly crash in Adamuz
Death toll likely to rise, local government spokesperson warns
At least 10 feared dead after collision in Toledo province
We are expecting to hear from Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente at the top of the hour, at 2pm local time (1pm UK).
Spain’s former labour minister Fátima Báñez was reportedly on one of the trains caught up in this morning’s crash.
Speaking just now on RTVE, Antonio Sanz, the Andalusia government’s emergency minister, confirmed she is believed to have been on board and has not yet been reached since the incident.
The death toll from today’s train collision has risen to 31, according to the latest information from local government in Castile-La Mancha.

All games of the first round of Spanish Copa del Rey football competition planned for today have been postponed as a mark of respect following the train crash in Urda, Spanish football federation said in a statement.
“The great Spanish football family remains united in grief over this tragedy, offering its support to the authorities to help the victims of this devastating accident,” the RFEF said in a statement.
A revised schedule will be published in due course.
The European Commission has offered to help with the investigation into today’s train crash in Urda.

“Our thoughts and our feelings are with the victims, their families and friends, and all those affected, and the Commission, together with the European Union Agency for Railways, is closely following the situation, and we stand ready to support the Spanish authorities in any way that may be needed.”
But she noted it was “too early, absolutely too early, to draw any conclusions” as the emergency response continues.
Von der Leyen has not yet spoken with Spain’s PM Pedro Sánchez this morning, the spokesperson said, who also pointed reporters to her message of solidarity on social media (11:32).
Today’s crash is already the fourth worst train accident in Spain recorded since the seventies – and the death toll is still expected to rise.
In 1972, 86 people died and 112 were injured in a head-on clash between two passenger trains in El Cuervo (Sevilla).
In 2013, 80 people died and more than 140 were injured in Angrois, Santiago de Compostela (A Coruña) after a high-speed train detailed outside the station.
And earlier this year, 46 people died and 152 were injured after two trains collided in Adamuz (Córdoba).
At least 30 people have died and 80 have been injured after two high-speed trains collided in Spain’s Toledo province, with fears the death toll could still rise higher (12:22).
The number of people affected is still expected to rise (10:46, 12:04), local authorities said, with growing concerns about a “major tragedy” (11:03).
The affected trains are understood to be Iryo 7076 with 146 passengers plus one baby on board, and AVE 2080 with 397 passengers on board, making it 544 people in total on board of both train (11:00).
Early inquiries point to a possible signalling failure that contributed to the crash, Spanish media reported (12:32).
The incident comes less than a year after a similar crash in Adamuz, the province of Córdoba, which killed 46 and injured 152 in January this year (11:00).
Spain’s high-speed railway network ranks as the largest in Europe and the second biggest in the world after China, carrying 25 million passengers in 2024.

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said he was “shocked” by the accident (11:05), with transport minister Óscar Puente working at the emergency control centre to “obtain all possible information about what happened” (11:16).
The Spanish king Felipe VI expressed his sorrow and solidarity with all affected (11:38, 12:07).

Meanwhile, El Mundo is reporting that the Iryo train flagged a failure in its LZB signalling system shortly before the crash, but the train behind did not receive the information due to a potential human error.
Investigators believe the AVE high-speed train travelling behind crashed into the stationary Iryo service, according to the newspaper.
The president of Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, is now briefing the reporters.

He confirms the latest figure of 30 dead – 24 in the AVE train and six in the Iryo train – but says the authorities expect this number to rise further as emergency services are yet to reach the most affected parts of the wreckage.
He also says some 80 people were injured, with 30 people with minor injuries, and 50 with moderate and more serious injuries of varying severity.
He thanks all emergency services for their help.

Unlike other party leaders, the far-right Vox party’s Santiago Abascal appears to be going ahead with his political plans for today as he continues campaigning ahead of next month’s parliamentary election in Spain.
In his comments, he repeatedly attacked Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez for “constantly putting the Spanish people at risk.”
He explicitly rejected calls to suspend the campaign, insisting that would only to “exploit the grief and mourning to silence complaints and protests regarding the decay of our infrastructure.”
Spanish King Felipe VI appeared in front of cameras on his visit to Bétera, where he is attending some military exercises.
His brief reaction was largely in line with his earlier written statement.
Visibly shaken, Felipe VI said he wanted to “express my deep regret over this horrific incident,” acknowledging “a high number of fatalities and many injuries.”

“My primary concern is to express my sorrow over this terrible tragedy and to convey our condolences, sadness, support, and affection to the families during such an incredibly difficult and painful time.”
He also thanked emergency services responding to the incident for their help.

items.title: Will Instagram's 90-minute videos make it impossible to switch off from socials?
paragraphs: It's official: the internet is eating itself. Instagram has just announced it's testing 90-minute video content, and my poor, brainrotted head cannot take it. Now, whether it's short-form, attention-stealing slop or long-form video rambling, it doesn't seem to matter to IG, as long as there's content.

Not to be a grandma, but I remember when the Instagram logo was a skeuomorphic vintage camera, so I feel I've earned the right to whinge. The app has evolved a lot since its debut, but the move to long-form video means yet another social media app is gunning for our precious attention, and I'm really feeling the fatigue.

On Monday, Instagram began testing the 90-minute clips with a handful of US-based creators. The 'Features' project has already been tested in Brazil and is aimed predominantly at podcasters and comedians. Whether other long-form creators will migrate from the safety of rival platforms like YouTube remains to be seen, but I already find the concept of extended video content on IG rather tiresome.

I'm a woman of structure. I like that TikTok is for brainrot and YouTube is for slightly more nuanced, long-form brainrot. But it's no secret that podcast content is ruling the social feed – it's cheap to produce, and so long as you can wrangle some semi-interesting yappers to host, you've got a steady flow of hour-long content each week.

I've already seen video content infiltrate my other precious apps like Spotify. Do I watch podcast videos on the platform? Absolutely not, but the fact that it's even there suggests I may be in the minority. Social media brands are competing to become the next 'every app', and with little distinction between them, it all feels a little like a desperate plea for my watch time.

I see a not-so-distant future where an evening can be swallowed by circling the drain of social media. 15 minutes on TikTok as an appetiser, catching up with your favourite zillenial podcasters on IG for main, and a nice YouTube video essay for dessert. Simply put, it's becoming too tempting to switch off.
For more social media news, check out Instagram's new brand identity that's more than just a wordmark, or take a look at the best social media platforms for artists and designers.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Flávio Bolsonaro on flight to Miami after fleeing Brazil amid election defeat
paragraphs: A jet carrying the far-right Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has left Guayaquil in Ecuador and is on its way to Miami, Florida, where it is expected to arrive mid-morning on Wednesday.

After losing Sunday night’s election to the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.

There, he boarded a Gulfstream IV registered as LV-JQW. The aircraft had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.

Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, boarded the jet with his wife and two daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador, and have continued to the Miami-Opa Locka executive airport. The senator is expected to hold a press conference in the US at some point on Wednesday.

A senior US state department official told media outlets that visas would be granted to Bolsonaro and his family, and on Tuesday night the US president said he would approve their move to the country.

“They’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Donald Trump said, as he returned from a campaign event in Texas. “I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well.”

Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.

Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him leaving the country.

There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies at about 6pm on Monday and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.
Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.

Shortly after the election result, police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.

Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.

O Globo newspaper reported that the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.

items.title: Mississippi residents say Musk’s xAI offered to buy homes if they don’t sue over datacenter noise
paragraphs: People in a Mississippi neighborhood, many of whom dislike a nearby power plant central to Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence ambitions, have received a stark offer – to sell their houses to his company and make way.

Real estate agents have been going door to door in Southaven, Mississippi, on behalf of xAI, Musk’s AI company that was folded into the SpaceX entity in February, touting a deal to purchase houses as long as the owners agree to not join a lawsuit against the company over the power plant’s noise.

This plan could potentially swallow up almost the entire neighborhood of Colonial Hills, on the western flank of Southaven. A realtor told one resident there is a target to purchase 418 homes, with 18 homeowners already agreeing to sell, according to a recording of a conversation heard by the Guardian. xAI did not respond to questions over these numbers and its plans for the neighborhood and has previously said it intends to be be a good neighbor; it denies all claims in the noise lawsuit.

The homes, the realtor and the local mayor say, will house xAI staff as the company continues its explosive expansion in the area, with three of its datacenters springing up in Southaven and adjoining Memphis, Tennessee, in just the past two years. This frantic pace, and the all-hours noise from gas turbines installed without permits to power the datacenters, has dismayed some locals.

“It sounds like an airplane engine but it’s continuous, it’s incredibly loud,” said Elizabeth Rose, a piano teacher, of the xAI site which sits about two miles from her home. “I’ve been woken up at 2am by it, I’ve been woken up at 3am by it. I sometimes have to just get away from it because it makes me so angry.”

Rose said she was shocked when the power plant, a former Duke Energy site housing 69 temporary gas turbines to feed the new datacenters, began its low-level growl in August last year. “All of a sudden there was a plant there,” she said. “And now I get the feeling they are trying to expand the buyout to the entire neighborhood. It will become Elon Musk’s little playground, basically. Elonville.”

The market value offers for these homes, in an area where the average house price is about $180,000, is a comparatively small outlay in creating the world’s largest cluster of AI supercomputers as envisioned by Musk, a technologist who is the world’s richest person and a major Republican donor.

Since July 2024, xAI has constructed three vast datacenters – called Colossus I, Colossus II and Macrohardrr – in the Memphis and Southaven conurbation, which sprawls across Tennessee’s border with Mississippi. Musk is currently spending up to four nights a week in an Airstream trailer in the Memphis area as he personally oversees the build-out of the datacenters to further develop the Grok AI chatbot.
“We’re seeing the fastest growth I’ve ever seen in my life for Grok bot,” Musk said during a SpaceX earnings call this month. “I’ve never seen anything grow this fast.”

Musk has spent around half a billion dollars helping elect Republicans in the last two election cycles and his zeal for datacenters is shared by Donald Trump, who has said anyone who opposes such development will become “backwards and poor”.

As is common in the broader grassroots backlash against datacenters, however, some residents in Southaven say they have been trampled upon in this gold rush. Three locals, anguished by the din of expansion, filed a lawsuit in June complaining of “near-constant noise, vibrations and other nuisance-level harms” from the nearby xAI power plant.

Jason Haley, one of the three plaintiffs, said he never considered himself an activist or political in any way but has been driven to distraction by the noise of the gas turbines that sit about half a mile from his home, which he has owned for the past 20 years.

“There’s a high-pitched hum and then another sound like an airplane over your house,” he said. “It’s been so torturous I can’t sleep, I just leave the house or turn on some music until I fall asleep completely exhausted. It drives you insane. You also lose hope because you’re being ignored or dismissed. There’s no escape.”

Exasperated by fruitless exchanges with Southaven’s mayor and enraged by Tate Reeves, the Republican, pro-AI Mississippi governor, claiming that a curb on datacenters are “surrendering the future of technology to China”, Haley lodged the lawsuit and started posting videos on social media of himself monitoring the rumbling noise levels.

“I thought I’d make some noise of my own because of this bullshit,” said Haley. “I didn’t know anything about Elon, still don’t know the man. But our governor saying I don’t love America because I don’t like being tortured by noise? That is just asinine and ignorant. We’ve got to hold people accountable when they are harming other people, I don’t care who you voted for, who you pray for or who your favorite team is.”

The allegations of heedless noise are denied by xAI, which has previously said that “we care deeply about being good neighbors” and has varied its power output and built sound-dampening walls. In a letter handed to nearby residents in Colonial Hills, MZX, the xAI subsidiary that operates the site, states that it “requires property for its business purposes” and is prepared to buy nearby houses with a contractual condition – that they do not join Haley’s class action lawsuit.

This offer is starting to see results. Since 9 October, five neighborhood homes have been bought by MZX, according to DeSoto county records. Gavin Foust, who lives near Haley and said his elderly neighbors have just agreed to sell, predicts more will follow.

“They are ideal neighbors and planned to live their rest of their lives in that house but they want to get out of Dodge now because they don’t want to be bothered by these turbines,” said Foust, who added he won’t accept the offer himself due to its requirement not to sue.
“My hearing was damaged when I was in the army but I can still hear this thing, it’s like a jet engine. Why would you put it in a city? Why push people out? It’s reckless and shameful.”

Foust, a paramedic, grew up in the unassuming western reaches of Southaven, a district filled with affordable, 1960s homes and quiet, close-knit communities. This serenity has been upended by the noise from the xAI power plant, he said, as well as its air pollution.

Dozens of temporary, truck-sized gas turbines have been running at the xAI premises without permits required by federal law, the US Environmental Protection Agency has determined. The EPA has also said the permit requirements are a matter for the state to enforce.

While no on-site air pollution monitoring has been done, the Southern Environmental Law Center estimated the toxic emissions from these turbines, which are typically highly polluting, have caused $44m in annual health costs.

In April, environmental groups and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) sued in federal court to stop use of the turbines, only for the US Department of Justice to unsuccessfully try to block the lawsuit by arguing xAI technology has been used to wage war on Iran and is therefore required for national security reasons.

“It’s been pretty shady from the get-go,” said Foust. “A lot of people in this neighborhood suffer from conditions exacerbated by all the nitrogen oxide, formaldehyde and other garbage put out by these turbines. For kids with asthma or elderly people with COPD [chronic obstructive pulmonary disease] it’s a mess all round. It’s pretty frustrating.”

In July, xAI agreed with state regulators to transform the power plant into a newer, permanent gas-fired facility by next summer, which should lessen the noise coming from the temporary turbines. Given the company’s repeated use of gas turbines without a federal permit and separate fines it may face for storm water violations, though, opponents remain wary.
“I’ve had hopes all along that haven’t come through,” said Haley. “The same company said it wasn’t polluting the air. I’m still hopeful but I’m not confident.”

The opposition to the datacenter influx hasn’t been universal, Haley acknowledged. Some locals aren’t too bothered by the noise while others actively champion the influx of cash into one of the poorest states in the union. Local businesses have experienced a surge in new activity, with the mayor hailing the datacenters for helping deliver new jobs and opportunity to the area.

“This development will produce unprecedented tax revenue for DeSoto county taxpayers that will enhance the quality of life for all,” said Darren Musselwhite, Southaven’s mayor, who oversaw a land swap deal with xAI that resulted in a new police and firefighter training center for the city.

“The buyout is not intended to be a company city at this point,” Musselwhite said of the property purchases. “This has never been mentioned to me. The buyout has multiple purposes which are to provide homes for some employees and a goodwill gesture from a good corporate citizen for those who perceive the industrial development near them as a negative.”

Musselwhite said dealing with the noise is a “top priority” for him but that city monitors have not detected a breach of a local noise ordinance limit of 70 decibels. Critics point to evidence that lower levels of noise, of 50 decibels or more like that recorded near the power plant, may be linked to adverse health impacts if persistent.

For those who can’t stand this noise, there is little to celebrate. Haley said the controversy has drawn the community together and made him question how AI is being “pushed down everyone’s throat”. He added: “Put it this way, I’m now registered to vote.” Rose, the piano teacher, said her roommate would accept three or four times the value of their home but she would still be opposed to such a sale.

“I wouldn’t take the offer if it was up to me, just to make things difficult for Elon,” she said. “I hate AI, I never understood why it was invented. I refuse to use it because I know touching it will cause that plant to crank up.”

items.title: Page\Park uses local stone and timber for school wellbeing hub in Edinburgh
paragraphs: Scottish architecture studio Page\Park has completed The Allardice Centre, a health and wellbeing hub for Fettes College in Edinburgh, which is topped with a lantern-like roof.

Named after the independent day and boarding school’s alumnus David Allardice, the 469-square-metre centre brings together medical and pastoral care services in a fully accessible building nestled into a wooded plot.

According to Page\Park, the centre’s design was informed by the late Allardice’s interest in Eastern philosophy, in particular the elemental philosophy of Wuxing, which led to a palette of timber, stone and metal.
The building’s structure is made from Scots-grown timber, while Darney stone quarried nearby forms the external load-bearing cladding, which is contrasted by a bronze roof.
“Allardice spent much of his working life in East Asia, and was drawn to ancient Chinese philosophy and the five essential elements, fire, water, wood, metal and earth,” the studio told Dezeen.

“This narrative directly influenced the design, materiality and construction approach, which can be seen through the strata-like stone cladding, burnt bronze metal roof, and connection to the outside,” it added.

The Allardice Centre is organised across a single storey, with an open wellbeing hub at its centre, wrapped by a series of individual treatment and counselling rooms overlooking the surrounding woodland.

Illuminating the central hub is a mono-pitched, lantern-like roof. This creates a ring of clerestory windows, framed by the exposed glued-laminated timber (glulam) structure designed in collaboration with Scottish engineering firm Will Rudd.

“Fitting the full brief for both medical and pastoral functions into this constrained site, while avoiding level changes to maximise accessibility, forced the plan to be quite deep,” explained the studio.

“Bringing natural light into this deep plan therefore became a challenge. To resolve this, the glulam structure extends and branches out at high level to reveal a triple-glazed clerestory lantern formed of timber curtain walling,” it added.

Inside The Allardice Centre, white walls allow the timber structure to come to the fore. In the treatment rooms, leaf-print and green fabrics create a visual connection to the surrounding site, which was developed by landscape architects Harrison Stevens.

“We were interested in the didactic implications of exposing the glulam timber frame, offering an insight into how the building was crafted, celebrating its sustainability principles and the elemental philosophy underpinning the design,” said the studio.

“The Darney stone chosen for the project was quarried only 75 kilometres away, and had fantastic mineral veins through it which paired neatly with the varying course sizes, leaning into the earth element theme, and giving a sense of permanence,” it added.
Other projects in Edinburgh recently featured on Dezeen include the extension of a Georgian townhouse by Pend, which complemented the existing stone structure with skinny red brickwork.
Elsewhere, Page\Park recently completed a teaching building for the University of Stirling, which was shortlisted for the 2025 RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award.
The photography is courtesy of Page\Park.

items.title: Israel's election too close to call. And, the Ebola outbreak reaches grim milestone
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-150313/nx-s1-mx-6020166-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Midterm ad spending has surpassed a record $11 billion, according to Ad Impact. An NPR analysis found that candidates in four major Senate races spent more than $15 million on fundraising ads in the 2025-26 election cycle. Meanwhile, President Trump has been campaigning in tight races across states like Texas, Mississippi, and Kansas.
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks during a campaign event on October 17, 2026 in Marietta, Georgia. Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images hide caption

The election in Israel is too close to call after voters turned out in record numbers to decide whether to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in office or oust him for an alternative. Netanyahu was in a tight race with his top rival Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff. Final vote tallies may take time, and if no bloc secures a majority, it could take days or weeks for party leaders to form a governing coalition and determine the next prime minister.
The Federal Reserve typically combats inflation by raising interest rates. While prices are currently rising faster than average wages, investors don't expect a rate hike at today's meeting.

The Ebola outbreak has surpassed 10,000 people infected since its declaration in May, according to the latest figures from the Democratic Republic of Congo. This outbreak has spread faster than any in history. It is also the largest in geographic scope, spanning from Nigeria to Kenya, and is second in death toll with nearly 5,000 deaths. Around one-third of those who have died have been children.

The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.

With Election Day less than a week away, Morning Edition's Michel Martin went to the Midwest to hear from voters about what is important to them this midterm cycle. In Springfield, Ohio, the Trump administration has conducted an aggressive campaign to deport Haitian residents who have been living legally in the country with Temporary Protected Status. The administration revoked TPS for Haitians during Trump's second term. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed has narrowly won the Democratic Senate nomination, a victory for the party's progressive wing. The swing state is important to both parties, which is why Trump and former President Barack Obama campaigned for their party's Senate candidate over the weekend.

As the holidays approach and appointments and commitments begin to pile up, author Caroline Sylge recommends a "say no" retreat — a day dedicated to figuring out which obligations you want to decline in the coming weeks and months. items.title: ‘Deceptively simple’: Gullah Geechee art exhibition illustrates that beauty lies in the details
paragraphs: In Time to Rejoice, a 2005 oil on canvas painting by artist Jonathan Green, nine women, each dressed in vibrantly colored shirts and skirts, with wide-brimmed hats obscuring their faces, gather in a clearing. They’re facing one woman who dances in the center, her arms outstretched, seemingly in ecstasy, a leg towards the sky. Her hat hovers off her head; only her face is visible, though, with her eyes closed, she doesn’t gaze at the viewer. It is an intimate scene, perhaps of sisters, friends or comrades.

The painting evokes a moment from Toni Morrison’s novel Beloved, in which Baby Suggs offers freedom and peace to formerly enslaved people who are gathered with her in a clearing: “In this here place, we flesh; flesh that weeps, laughs; flesh that dances on bare feet in grass. Love it. Love it hard. Yonder they do not love your flesh. They despise it … And O my people they do not love your hands. Those they only use, tie, bind, chop off and leave empty. Love your hands! Love them. Raise them up and kiss them … and all your inside parts that they’d just as soon slop for hogs, you got to love them. The dark, dark liver – love it, love it and the beat and beating heart, love that too.”

Time to Rejoice is curator Ben Billingsley’s favorite in the Cameron Art Museum’s new exhibition, Rooted in Memory: The Gullah Geechee Vision of Jonathan Green, on view now through 24 January in Wilmington, North Carolina.

“You can see that they’re wearing blue chains, very contemporary kinds of clothing,” Billingsley said. “So suddenly this is not the 18th century, this is not the 19th century, this is here and now. It really ties together the contemporary culture to this longstanding tradition that has been there since these people arrived on these shores.”
Green was born in Gardens Corner, South Carolina, and trained at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. His Gullah Geechee heritage greatly informs his work.

An anonymous family of donor members of the museum has collected Green’s work for three generations. The family temporarily loaned some of their personal collection to the museum, allowing them to “not only honor [Green’s] work, but also show the behind the scenes of how a collection develops and how generational collecting can develop over time”, Billingsley said.

As the museum was creating the exhibition, Billingsley realized that it made sense to include art and objects that highlight the broader Gullah Geechee culture. The resulting exhibition, which ties together contemporary art and history, also includes traditional Gullah Geechee creations, such as sweet grass baskets, quilts and Gullah dolls. The museum also received works on loan from the South Carolina State Museum, the Gibbes Museum and the Charleston Museum for the exhibition.

In some ways, the art is “deceptively simple”, Billingsley said. It’s easy to look at Green’s work, to process the full image. But the more viewers sit with the work and take it in, the more detail they discover.

“There are hundreds of brushstrokes per square inch, and the deeper you get into looking at them, the more you start to uncover what I think he’s really saying about his own experience and the experience of the people that he paints,” he said.
Rooted in Memory includes some of Green’s paintings of women, which Billingsley said, “create an interesting tension”.

“Most of the time, the women’s faces are somewhat obscured – either they have their back to the viewer or maybe they’re looking down, they may have a hat brim covering the face,” he said. “It makes me want to know what they’re doing, what they are thinking. It also allows them to somewhat be almost like universal avatars. You can imagine people you know in your life in that scenario because of the degree of anonymity in the face, especially if you’re in the rural south-east of the country. It very much feels like familiar territory.”

Included in the exhibition are four watercolors by Green that diverge from his traditional style and stand out in contrast to his other work. The watercolors are costume designs that Green was commissioned to paint for the Sapelo festival for a production of Porgy and Bess.

“His inspiration for these was to imagine what if the fashion, the fabric traditions, the printing traditions, weaving traditions from west Africa had come into our culture, not through forced labor and forced arrival,” Billingsley said. “But if they had arrived here through willing immigrants who continued to bring their culture into the contemporary mainstream.”

items.title: Dezeen Awards public vote reveals 16 winning designs
paragraphs: The results of the design public vote for Dezeen Awards 2026 have been revealed, with 16 design projects selected as winners by Dezeen’s readers.
Projects voted as readers’ favourite include a temporary festival venue made from an eclectic mix of salvaged materials, including fabric from hot air balloons and sheep’s wool.
Another public vote winner is a set of jacquard textiles composed like music to create layered spatial compositions.
Dezeen Awards 2026 public vote winners revealed this week
Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, will reveal all public vote winners this week. The architecture winners were announced on Monday and the interiors shortlist was announced yesterday.
Readers were invited to choose their favourite projects out of the 392-strong shortlist in this year’s vote.
The vote took place between 28 September and 16 October, spanning shortlists in each of Dezeen Awards’ three main category sectors.
All the winning design projects are listed below, each with a link to a dedicated page on the Dezeen Awards website where you can find an image and more information about the project.

items.title: Coca-Cola gives everyday heroes the royal treatment in posh portrait campaign
paragraphs: Coca-Cola has launched a wholesome new campaign honouring the local business people who support it. Local Royalty features four hand-painted portraits created by real royal portrait artists, proving that honour doesn't have to be dictated by blood.

While many ad campaigns are focusing on the digital side of design, it's a refreshing change to see Coca-Cola embracing analogue art. A campaign with heart and intention, Local Royalty demonstrates how stripping back to the tactile can create some of the best adverts.

The four portrait subjects were chosen to represent everyday people from hospitality and retail, including workers from a pub, corner shop, café, and fish and chip shop. Painted by artists who have previously captured royals such as Queen Elizabeth II, King Charles III, the Prince and Princess of Wales and Princess Anne, the stately portraits are a wonderfully unexpected homage to life's everyday heroes.

“Independent business owners create the places where local life happens, yet their contribution often goes unrecognised," says Rhona Stephen, senior director, communications for Coca-Cola Great Britain. "With Local Royalty, we wanted to celebrate them in a way that felt deliberately unexpected and enduring. By borrowing the visual language of official portraiture and placing these owners at its centre, the campaign gives their everyday impact the status it deserves.”

The portraits will be displayed as part of a free public exhibition at the Saatchi Gallery in London from 28th October to 1st November. For more creative news, check out Coca-Cola's new look or take a look at our guide on how to stand out as a portrait artist.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Luminous viewpoint by Ryue Nishizawa rises within Japanese landfill site
paragraphs: A giant orange cone designed by Japanese architect Ryue Nishizawa acts as an observation deck at this large recycling complex on Shikoku island in Japan.

Nishizawa, co-founder of Japanese studio SANAA, positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin at Oono Associates, a recycling complex in the city of Toon, and open up this closed-off industrial space to the public.
Named Observatory, it was created for the inaugural edition of Setouchi Art and Industry 2026, an art and architecture festival held across industrial sites in Japan.

Specifically, it forms part of the Landscapes of Waste – A landscape shaped by nature, industry, and people exhibition, curated by Nishizawa’s studio partner Kazuyo Sejima, with whom he founded SANAA in 1995.
Nishizawa positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin within the vast recycling complex in Toon, Ehime, revealing the closed-off industrial setting to the public.
The bright orange cone measures 33 metres in diameter and four metres in height. Its size was intended to emulate an artificial hill.
Its luminous orange finish was chosen to deliberately contrast the blue-green hues of the surrounding landfill lining and landscape beyond it.
The platform encourages visitors to observe how the landscape is shaped by nature and human activity, and experience the processes of material circulation at the recycling plant.

Alongside Nishizawa’s observation platform, the Landscapes of Waste exhibition includes bus stops by architectural studio Shingo Masuda + Katsuhisa Otsubo, as well as buses and visitor workwear by Suzuko Yamada Architects.
Visitors are required to take these buses to the site and put on the workwear, as seen in the photos. The festival team said this brings “visitors themselves into the composition of the landscape”.
“Together, these interventions invite a closer encounter with the relationship between nature, industrial infrastructure and human activity,” it added.

Setouchi Art and Industry 2026 was organised by the Japan Industrial Art Foundation. Artists and architects were invited to work with industrial sites across Okayama and the Ehime prefecture on Shikoku to create a “decentralised museum” that opens these settings to the public.
Its inaugural edition runs until 31 October across seven venues, which also include a salt production site, a textile factory, a shipbuilder and a battery manufacturer.

“Developed through collaboration between artists and participating companies, the exhibitions offer access to industrial spaces usually closed to the public, revealing the technologies, materials and people behind everyday life,” said Setouchi Art and Industry.

“We hope that many people, including the younger generation, will re-examine Japan’s industries from a fresh perspective and discover the charm and potential hidden within them,” added Japan Industrial Art Foundation director Masahiro Ito.
Other recent projects by SANAA include the Taichung Green Museumbrary in Taiwan and a proposal for the National Museum of Ecuador.

items.title: At least 30 dead in crash between two trains in central Spain, media say
paragraphs: The scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press via AP hide caption

BARCELONA, Spain — A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 30 people on Wednesday in central Spain, according to local media.
Spanish authorities initially reported 10 deaths, but Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, added "that number will surely rise."
Spanish state-owned news agency EFE and other media reported later that the death toll had risen to at least 30.
It was the second major train accident in Spain this year.
Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Padilla told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain. One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. She said the cause of the crash was not known.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mónica García told TVE that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.

The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. It appeared the RENFE train rammed the IRYO train, Spanish media reported. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities."

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to injured passengers.
A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police to the crash site.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cancelled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo."
"Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families."
The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, wrote on X that he was on his way to the crash site.

In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

items.title: A US woman feared dead was reported alive in Mexico. But cops now say that isn’t true
paragraphs: Arizona authorities say their Mexican counterparts were resoundingly mistaken when they publicly claimed recently that they found alive a woman who was feared slain after disappearing in 2024 – a turn of events that her sister has called “turmoil” and “heartbreaking”.
The case in question centers on Shayna Feinman, who was reported missing in rural Yavapai county, Arizona, in March 2024 at age 38.

Authorities believe she was walking to an acquaintance’s home when she was last seen – but she never arrived or returned to her dog, as the Arizona news outlet KSAZ reported. An ensuing search turned up Feinman’s car abandoned near where she had been staying with her boyfriend, Cavett Richards, according to the station.
Her wallet and identification reportedly were inside the vehicle, and her cellphone was ultimately recovered on nearby land.

Although Feinman had not been found, the Yavapai county sheriff’s office subsequently charged Richards as well as a man named William DalCerro with second-degree murder, conspiracy and concealing a corpse in connection with her disappearance. But the charges were dismissed, a $20,000 reward being offered for information as authorities kept investigating the case.

The secretariat for security and citizen protection in the Mexican municipality of Tijuana then delivered what initially appeared to be a startling update in Feinman’s case on Saturday, saying in a statement that she had been located in the city’s Encino neighborhood the previous day.

The statement from the secretariat had a picture of the woman sitting in front of a desk atop which was a missing poster with Feinman’s information. It asserted without elaborating that investigators had confirmed Feinman’s identity, noting that her physical characteristics matched those listed in her missing person report.

The woman had been put in protective custody while Tijuana authorities arranged for her to speak with the Feinman family and US consular officials, the statement said. The agency went so far as to post a link to its Saturday statement on a social media page belonging to Feinman’s sister, Kara.
But both Kara Feinman and the Yavapai’s sheriff’s office met the Tijuana officials’ statement with evident skepticism.
Kara told KSAZ in a story published on Monday that she was waiting for the Yavapai sheriff’s office “to know for certain” that Shayna had been found.

Though she acknowledged the woman in the picture released by Tijuana officials had “similar physical attributes” to Shayna, Kara struck a cautious tone, telling KSAZ: “I can only hope and pray [for] good news – but right now, we have to be realistic.”

Meanwhile, a sheriff’s office spokesperson told KSAZ that the agency was “aware of reports indicating that Shayna Feinman may have been located in Mexico” – but “at this time, the information remains unconfirmed”.

“There is insufficient evidence to verify her identity,” Yavapai sheriff’s office spokesperson Paul Wick added to KSAZ. Wick said the sheriff’s office was “actively investigating the matter” and would provide an update as soon as one could be “confirmed and … released”.

The Yavapai sheriff’s office published that update on Tuesday, when it said in a statement: “Today, US authorities confirmed to [office] detectives, utilizing physical evidence, that the individual located is not Shayna Feinman.”

The sheriff’s office alluded to prior media reports “regarding the alleged discovery of Shayna Feinman” that “were published without official law enforcement confirmation” – before saying its “detectives continue to work diligently with [her] family during this stressful time”.
Tijuana’s security and citizen protection secretariat did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In an interview with the Guardian on Tuesday, Kara Feinman said she believed the confusion about her sister possibly being in Tijuana initially stemmed from at least one concerned citizen who became convinced that she was there and made that known on social media.

She described being guarded about that possibility, reluctantly opening her mind in light of the Tijuana secretariat’s claims – and then enduring cyberbullying online by users who harshly judged her for not reacting effusively enough to the ultimately false news that Shayna had been found alive.

As she processed the reality that the search for the truth about her sister’s disappearance continued, Kara Feinman said her hope now was for those passionate about such investigations to realize how harmful it can be “jumping to conclusions without having all of the information” and then directing harsh words at the people most affected by those cases.
“Words are stronger than people think, and kindness can go so far,” Kara Feinman said. “It’s been turmoil going through this.
“It’s heartbreaking. It’s terrible, and I don’t wish this on anybody.”

items.title: XPPen Magic Pro 13 review: a premium Android drawing tablet for work and play
paragraphs: The Magic Pro 13 is a superb portable Android drawing tablet with an excellent pen and a simple connection to a PC, offering a premium experience whether mobile or at your desk.
Matt nano-etched glass with a paper-like feel, at 120Hz
Plugs into a PC as a drawing display over USB-C
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

I liked the original XPPen Magic Drawing Pad because it showed that an Android tablet could be built around artists' needs. Its drawing surface felt closer to a desktop tablet than the glossy, slippery screens on most consumer devices, like an iPad or Samsung's Galaxy Tab series (read our guide to the best tablets with a stylus pen for drawing). I used it as a loose sketching tool, but accuracy issues kept me from replacing my desktop tablet, and I soon went back to my iPad Pro.

Three years on, and XPPen's new Magic Pro 13 fixes the biggest issues I had with the older first-time model. It has a processor that handles demanding art apps, a new stylus (importantly with 5,080 LPI resolution), a 3K 120Hz screen, and a USB-C connection that turns it into a PC drawing display. It’s also a good everyday Android tablet for video, email and Google Docs.

Wacom’s MovinkPad Pro 14 currently leads this category, and Huion’s Kamvas Pad 12 undercuts both, though its performance comes at the cost of a less impressive processor. The Magic Pro 13 sits closer to Wacom and Apple than the brand's old ‘budget tablet’ reputation, and it makes a strong case to be the one you pick, based on price, specs, and performance.

XPPen has come a long way from a disruptor to a genuinely impressive drawing tablet manufacturer; for example, its recent Artist Ultra 14 OLED tablet is an advanced desktop drawing tablet. The pitch with the Magic Pro 13 is that the same tech, minus OLED, can fit into an Android tablet.

Opening the box, I'm struck that XPPen hasn't overloaded the package with extras for the first time; you get the tablet, spare nibs, a drawing glove, and a high-quality USB-C cable for charging and PC connectivity. A case or stand would have been welcome, but that would have bumped the cost; besides, XPPen sells a stand, case, and magnetic keyboard separately, just like Apple.

A close look at the new tablet reveals a premium-feeling product. The white frame, curved edges, flat matte display, and discreet buttons make the Magic Pro 13's design choices closer to Wacom and Apple than the budget end of the market. At 655g and 6.65mm, it’s easy to hold for long stretches, which matters when you’re not propping it on a desk. I took it outside to sketch a local lane and also used it on the sofa, and it suits both.

The 12.95-inch screen gives you room to paint comfortably. For long, detailed desk sessions, some artists prefer a larger display; for example, you don't get the space to rest your wrist as you do with a desktop design, but as a tablet for all occasions, it's a nice size.

The Magic Pro 13 has two USB-C ports, but only one supports the high-bandwidth video connection needed for PC mode, so make sure you plug into the right one. Storage is expandable by microSD, which helps if you collect reference images and large art files. There are some quirks to the design; for example, XPPen has chosen to keep the rear camera that comes on standard tablets, a small lens in the top corner of the rear panel, which I thought could make drawing on the screen when laid flat a little awkward, expecting a slump or wobble, but it never happened.

The nano-etched glass has a matte, paper-like finish with a little resistance under the nib. The 3K panel covers 100% sRGB and 96% DCI-P3, with a peak brightness of 650 nits. At 120Hz, marks keep up with the pen, so it feels natural. The tablet display can toggle between 120Hz, 90Hz, and 60Hz, so you can balance battery life to how you use it; 60Hz, for example, is fine for browsing, and 120Hz is ideal for digital painting.

The X4 Smart Chip Stylus offers 16,384 pressure levels, a 2g initial activation force and 60 degrees of tilt. The 5,080 LPI figure is worth noting: it measures how finely the tablet resolves pen movement, separate from the number of pressure steps, and this is double the resolution of the original Magic Drawing Pad and on par with most high-end desktop drawing tablets.
The pen has enough weight to feel sturdy without tiring my hand; I draw for around two hours at a time and never get the kind of cramp that can creep in with slim styluses or cheaper, lighter pens.

To test tracking, I drew small circles, tapped dots, scribbled brush strokes, and repeatedly overdrew the same line. Lines stayed smooth, the cursor followed the nib, and I saw no jitter. That’s where the original Magic Drawing Pad fell short, and some recent budget tablets, like the Kamvas Pad 12, too. Side by side with Wacom’s Pro Pen 3, I couldn’t pick a difference.

My go-to Android drawing app is ArtRage (ArtRage 6 is on XPPen's free install list, but I use ArtRage Vitae); it's an older painting simulator with excellent traditional-media brushes and heavy paint tools that show quickly whether a tablet can keep up. I painted a quick sketch of a lane near my house, switching brushes and pushing paint around with the heavier tools. There was no visible lag, strokes landed where I aimed, and overall it's a really nice experience, close to using a desktop tablet.

The Dimensity 8300 processor, 8GB of RAM, and Android 16 handle painting and illustration well. Wacom’s MovinkPad Pro 14 offers 12GB, which gives it an edge with very large files. I tested the 3D sculpting app Nomad Sculpt on the tablet, and it was fine, with no issues; unlike the new budget Huion Kamvas Pad 12, the Magic Pro 13 didn’t get warm or have any issues, even in Performance mode. I’m not one for using massive amounts of layers; I rarely get past three and tend to collapse them regularly, but even when I did decide to add 10 layers and duplicate my painting to see what would happen, there was no slowdown or warming.

A key feature of the Magic Pro 13 is that it works as a standalone Android tablet and as a drawing display for a desktop or laptop. I plugged in the included USB-C cable, and it connected as a display, with the hardware handling the video link. I use an HP Omen Max 16 for gaming and art, and it worked seamlessly, with no need to download drivers or fiddle with the laptop or tablet settings.

Wacom’s MovinkPad Pro 14 offers a similar workflow, wired or over Wi-Fi, but it relies on a companion app on the PC to get it working. A wired connection also means turning on Developer mode and USB debugging on the tablet first. Those are one-off steps, and XPPen doesn’t offer a wireless option, but the XPPen route requires less setup and is literally a 'plug and go' solution.

I drew on the Magic Pro 13 away from my desk, then connected it to my computer to use my desktop art software, moving from ArtRage Vitae and into Rebelle. If you work at a desk all day, you’ll want a bigger screen, but for home work, travel, or hobbyists like myself who can’t justify both a tablet and a pen display, it covers both jobs really well.

The Magic Pro 13 ships with ibisPaint X and XPPen’s own Canvas app. I still prefer ArtRage for painting. Canvas adds Quick Draw, which wakes the tablet straight into sketching, and a doodle tool for annotating photos. It also keeps reference images from my shelf available alongside other work.

Split-screen and multi-app use work as you’d expect on Android 16, so I can check email or a web page mid-painting and return without losing my place. Performance mode suits artwork and demanding video, while Comfort mode cuts heat and suits browsing and Google Docs, though I didn't notice any heat during extended use.

The 13MP rear and 8MP front cameras cover video calls and reference snaps. I’ve been using the Magic Pro 13 on and off for three weeks, from general browsing to art creation; generally, the battery has lasted a couple of days before needing a charge.

The Wacom MovinkPad Pro 14 has a larger 14-inch OLED display with deeper blacks and 900 nits of peak brightness, plus a Snapdragon 8s Gen 3 chip and 12GB of RAM. It can also connect to a PC wirelessly (but, as mentioned, you need a companion app, since it's not a hardware solution). If screen quality, desk space, or a wireless link matters most to you, buy the Wacom.

By contrast, the new XPPen Magic Pro 13 costs around $100 / £100 less, has cameras the Wacom lacks, and connects to a PC through a hardware-level USB-C video link rather than a companion app for an easy solution. The recently released Huion Kamvas Pad 12 is cheaper, but the Magic Pro 13 sits a tier above it in screen, pen, and processing power – it's altogether closer to the experience of using MovinkPad Pro 14 or even an iPad Air.

The bottom line is that the new Magic Pro 13 is an accomplished, premium Android tablet with artists' needs at the centre of its design and workflow. If you want one tablet for drawing on the move and at a desk, this does the job: the stylus and screen feel natural, the original's tracking problems are gone, and it connects to a PC quickly. The Magic Pro 13 is the best option yet for artists looking beyond an iPad for an Android tablet, if you can live without the Wacom's OLED.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.
